Well, doctor, it’s a bit of a long story, but I suppose what really brings me in today is this whole situation with the local historical society. I’ve been a member for years, you know, just helping out here and there, mostly with the bake sales and the archives. But recently, they mentioned needing to raise funds for the roof repair on the old schoolhouse, and I just... I don't know, I felt this incredible surge of energy about it. I stood right up in the meeting and basically volunteered to run the entire fundraiser myself. And I mean the *entire* thing. 

I went home that very afternoon and started sketching out these elaborate quilt designs—five different patterns, mind you, all historically accurate to the 1880s—thinking we could auction them off. I was up half the night just looking at fabric swatches and historical records. Then, the next morning, practically at the crack of dawn, I started calling every volunteer on our roster. I was making these incredibly detailed schedules, color-coded and everything, assigning people to shifts for the next three months. I even called the mayor's office to see if we could block off Main Street for a parade, which, in hindsight, was maybe a bit much.

But at the time, it all made perfect sense! I was promising everyone these absolutely impossible deadlines, telling them we’d have the quilts done in a week and the whole town mobilized by Friday. I felt like I could do it all, like I didn't even need to sleep or eat, just work on this project. But now... well, my husband had to practically drag me in here because I’m completely overwhelmed, the living room is covered in fabric scraps and charts, and I haven't actually finished a single quilt block. I just took on so much, so fast, and I couldn't stop myself.

Well, yes, absolutely, people definitely noticed, because... well, the way I felt during that time was just so intense. At the very beginning of it all, I felt... oh, how do I even describe it? It was like they were moving in slow motion and I was running at top speed, and I just couldn't tolerate anyone dragging their feet. Well, my appetite has been just completely gone, honestly. I used to love cooking, especially making these big Sunday dinners for Tom and the grandkids—pot roast, mashed potatoes, the whole nine yards—but lately, just the thought of food makes me feel slightly sick. Tom will make me a sandwich and I'll just stare at it until the bread gets stale. And my concentration... oh, it's just shot. Completely shot. I tried to sit down and read a magazine the other day, just a simple home and garden magazine, and I found myself reading the same paragraph over and over again for twenty minutes without absorbing a single word. It’s like my brain is just wrapped in thick, heavy cotton wool.

And as for... well, as for the other thing you asked about. The thoughts about death. It's... it's hard to talk about, doctor, it really is. I want to be clear, I don't have a plan to hurt myself. I could never do that to Tom, or the girls, I just couldn't. I'm not sitting here figuring out ways to end it all. But... well, I do catch myself thinking, especially when I'm lying awake at three in the morning and all the guilt about the quilt orders and the historical society is just crushing me... I catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up. Just went to sleep and didn't open my eyes again.

I would just be buzzing around him while he was trying to watch his program. It wasn't just a fleeting thought, it was this absolute necessity to be active, to be doing, doing, doing. It was this wonderful, radiant feeling, like a light had been switched on inside my head and suddenly every single idea I had was just brilliant. I mean, I would come up with a plan for a new quilt pattern or a way to organize the historical society archives, and it just seemed so obviously wonderful and perfect. I felt like I was finally seeing things clearly and everyone else was just... well, catching up. \n\nBut, you know, the funny thing is, as wonderful as I felt, if anyone—and I mean anyone—tried to question my ideas or even suggest we slow down a bit... oh, I would just turn on a dime. I just felt this intense irritation, this feeling that they were all just standing in my way, deliberately trying to hold me back from doing these amazing things. It was like they were moving in slow motion and I was running at top speed, and I just couldn't tolerate anyone dragging their feet. Well, yes, absolutely. It was... it was very different from how I normally am, and it certainly lasted more than a week. It was that whole five-month stretch I was telling you about with the heritage quilts.

After all that running around and all those brilliant ideas, I just crashed. I have these beautiful heirloom tomatoes and a whole bed of dahlias that I've cultivated for years. I would usually be out there at the crack of dawn with my coffee, just enjoying the quiet and pulling a weed or two. And my quilting! Oh, I've entered a quilt in the county fair every year since 1998. I usually spend hours planning the patterns and picking out just the right calico prints. \n\nBut after those five months were over... I just stopped caring. I would sit in the kitchen, and Tom would bring in the mail, and there would be my new seed catalogs and the latest fabric swatches I had ordered, and... nothing. I would just look at them sitting there on the kitchen table and I wouldn't feel a single thing. No excitement, no inspiration, just this heavy, blank nothingness. I didn't even want to open the envelopes. It was like I was looking at someone else's mail. I just couldn't muster up an ounce of interest in the things that used to bring me so much joy, and it just broke my heart, it really did.\n\nDoctor: After you felt that intense low period following the five-month stretch, did you feel like you eventually came out of it and returned to feeling more like your usual self, or have you been struggling with that depression up until coming in here today?\n\nPatient: Oh, doctor, I wish I could tell you that I just snapped out of it and went right back to my garden and my sewing machine, I really do. Oh, my goodness, yes. Racing almost sounds too calm a word for it, to be perfectly honest with you. It was more like... well, you know how it looks when someone is sitting in front of the television with the remote control, just flipping through the channels as fast as their thumb can push the button? I’d be frantically trying to remember if Mrs. Higgins had pledged fifty dollars or a hundred, or if we needed to send a formal thank-you note to the hardware store for their contribution. And then, without even taking a breath, my thoughts would completely switch gears again to the church announcements for Sunday, worrying about who was supposed to bring the potato salad for the fellowship hour and if I needed to call the pastor to make sure the quilt project was printed in the morning bulletin. 

It was just quilt blocks to donor lists to church announcements, over and over, spinning so quickly that I couldn't hold one thought long enough to actually finish it! I'd start a sentence to poor Tom about the fabric dye, and halfway through the breath I'd be talking about the church bake sale, and he would just look at me like I was speaking absolute gibberish. I just couldn't slow it down, doctor. It was like I was on a runaway train of my own ideas, and I just had to hold on for dear life while my brain just kept jumping and jumping and jumping. I remember one Tuesday, I had spread out all the files on the floor to try and organize them, but I couldn't even sort one single pile because every time I picked up a paper, my brain was already five miles down the road on a completely different topic!

Oh, heavens, yes. Yes, I was talking... well, talking doesn't even really cover it. It was more like a flood, just a constant stream of words coming out of my mouth. I remember, specifically, we had these committee meetings—usually we just meet once a month at the public library, you know, in that little back room near the genealogy section? Well, during those months, I was calling meetings constantly. And when we were in those meetings, I would just take over completely. 

I would stand up there at the front of the table and I would talk so fast... just incredibly fast, rattling off everything all at once. I’d be going on and on about the quilt patterns, and then right into the budgets for the backing and the thread, and then immediately into my plans for the publicity, like how we needed to contact the regional newspapers and maybe even get a spot on the morning news in the city. I had it all mapped out in my head, and I just had to get it all out.

And the other ladies... well, they would try to interrupt. I remember Clara—she's been the committee secretary for fifteen years—she kept raising her hand, or she'd lean forward and say, "Mary, dear, if we could just look at the agenda..." but I couldn't even let her finish her sentence! I just talked right over her. They would all try to get a word in edgewise, just to ask a simple question or try to slow me down, and I just kept going. I literally couldn't stop. It felt... it felt impossible to stop. 

Like, if I closed my mouth for even one second, all those brilliant ideas were just going to explode right out of my ears! So I just kept talking and talking, faster and faster, until I was practically breathless, and everyone else was just sitting there staring at me like I was a complete stranger. I just... I had so much to say, and it all had to come out right that very second, you know? It's so embarrassing to think about now, how I wouldn't let anyone else speak, but at the time, stopping just wasn't an option. I just couldn't do it.

Oh, heavens, no. No, I wouldn't say I did anything like that at all. I mean, spending sprees? Poor Tom would have an absolute heart attack if I tried something like that! We've been very careful with our budget ever since he retired, and I've always been the one who sits down at the kitchen table every Sunday evening to balance the checkbook to the very penny. But I only ever bought what was strictly necessary, and I always made sure to buy it when it was on sale, keeping every single receipt in a little manila envelope so the committee could reimburse me properly from the project fund. I certainly wasn't going out and buying fancy jewelry or booking flights to Europe or anything crazy like that! 

And reckless driving? Oh, absolutely not. I am a very cautious driver, doctor. I’ve driven the exact same routes around this town for thirty years, and I am terrified of getting a speeding ticket. Even on the days when my mind was just racing a mile a minute and I was absolutely desperate to get to the library for our committee meetings, I still stopped at every single yellow light. I remember one Tuesday afternoon, I was practically vibrating with excitement because I had just had a complete revelation about how to piece together the backing fabric, and I was hurrying down Elm Street, but I still came to a complete stop to let Mrs. Gable's old tabby cat cross the road near the Methodist church. I just couldn't bear the thought of being careless, no matter how fast my brain was going.

As for making big decisions without thinking them through... well, the biggest decisions I was making were entirely about the quilt patterns and the historical society's timeline. I suppose to me, right then in the moment, deciding between a sawtooth border and a scalloped edge felt like a monumental, life-altering choice that had to be made that very second! But it wasn't a real risk, you know? It wasn't like I was signing away our mortgage or quitting a job or doing anything that would actually ruin our lives. So, no, despite all that wild energy and the constant talking and the not sleeping, I wasn't doing anything dangerous. I was still just keeping to my usual rules and routines, I was just... well, I was just doing them all at a hundred miles an hour!

I remember, specifically, we had these committee meetings—usually we just meet once a month at the public library, you know, in that little back room near the genealogy section? I’d be going on and on about the quilt patterns, and then right into the budgets for the backing and the thread, and then immediately into my plans for the publicity, like how we needed to contact the regional newspapers and maybe even get a spot on the morning news in the city. I just talked right over her. They would all try to get a word in edgewise, just to ask a simple question or try to slow me down, and I just kept going. I literally couldn't stop. It's so embarrassing to think about now, how I wouldn't let anyone else speak, but at the time, stopping just wasn't an option. No, I wouldn't say I did anything like that at all. I mean, spending sprees? Poor Tom would have an absolute heart attack if I tried something like that! We've been very careful with our budget ever since he retired, and I've always been the one who sits down at the kitchen table every Sunday evening to balance the checkbook to the very penny. Even during those months when I was so incredibly wound up about the heritage project, I never once touched our personal savings. \n\nI will admit, I was making quite a few trips to the fabric store—probably three or four times a week at one point, because I kept realizing we needed more of this very specific navy blue cotton blend for the sashing between the quilt blocks. I remember one Tuesday afternoon, I was practically vibrating with excitement because I had just had a complete revelation about how to piece together the backing fabric, and I was hurrying down Elm Street, but I still came to a complete stop to let Mrs. Gable's old tabby cat cross the road near the Methodist church. I just couldn't bear the thought of being careless, no matter how fast my brain was going.\n\nAs for making big decisions without thinking them through... well, the biggest decisions I was making were entirely about the quilt patterns and the historical society's timeline. I suppose to me, right then in the moment, deciding between a sawtooth border and a scalloped edge felt like a monumental, life-altering choice that had to be made that very second! But it wasn't a real risk, you know? It wasn't like I was signing away our mortgage or quitting a job or doing anything that would actually ruin our lives. So, no, despite all that wild energy and the constant talking and the not sleeping, I wasn't doing anything dangerous. I was still just keeping to my usual rules and routines, I was just... well, I was just doing them all at a hundred miles an hour!"
